'''John Gordon Skellam''' (1914-1979) was a [[statistician]] and [[ecologist]], who discovered the [[Skellam distribution]].

Skellam was born in [[Staffordshire]]. He was educated at [[Hanley, Staffordshire|Hanley]] High School where he won several scholarships including free admission to [[New College, Oxford|New College in Oxford]]. He was one of the most respected members of the British Region of the [[International Biometric Society|Biometric Society]].<ref>{{cite journal | title = Obituary: G. Lefort 1921-1979 | journal = Biometrics | volume = 36 | issue = 3 | pages = 557–559 | publisher = International Biometric Society | jstor = 2530230}}</ref>

In 1951, John G. Skellam developed the [[reaction–diffusion system|reaction-diffusion]] model of [[Invasion biology terminology|invasion biology]]. This model describes the dynamics of populations, which simultaneously develops and spreads, and provides that the invasion front moves with constant speed.<ref>{{ cite book | title = The Princeton Guide to Ecology |editor=Simon A. Levin |editor2=Stephen R. Carpenter |editor3=H. Charles J. Godfray |editor4=Ann P. Kinzig |editor5=Michel Loreau |editor6=Jonathan B. Losos |editor7=Brian Walker |editor8=David S. Wilcove | publisher = Princeton University Press | date = Jul 27, 2009 | chapter = Milestones in Ecology | author = Christopher Morris | url = http://press.princeton.edu/chapters/s9_m8879.pdf }}</ref> He explained on the basis of habitation [[muskrat]] introduced to [[Europe]] that only by chance the species may be in a place where it would have to grow.<ref>{{Cite web| title=Biological Invasions in Heterogeneous Environments | author1=Tom Robbins | author2=Mark Lewis | url=http://www.math.utah.edu/~robbins/research/UofA_mathbio.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070225141858/http://www.math.utah.edu:80/%7Erobbins/research/UofA_mathbio.pdf | archive-date=2007-02-25}}</ref>

Skellam has provided a model that allows to take the dynamics of populations as a [[random variable]] at any time t. Its [[Stochastic process|stochastic form]] is much more flexible than previous deterministic equations.<ref>{{cite journal | title = Insects and Insect Ecology | last1 = Strickland | first1 = A.H. | volume = 3 | year = 1957 | journal = New Scientist | pages = 17–20 }}</ref>
